extraction.name: OpenBookQA
extraction.description: OpenBookQA is a question answering dataset modeled after open book exams for assessing human understanding of a subject. It consists of 5,957 4-way multiple-choice questions probing elementary science facts and their application to novel situations, paired with a core set of 1,326 elementary level science facts and an auxiliary set of about 6,000 additional facts.
extraction.creator: Todor Mihaylov, Peter Clark, Tushar Khot, Ashish Sabharwal
extraction.citeAs: Mihaylov, T., Clark, P., Khot, T., & Sabharwal, A. (2018). Can a Suit of Armor Conduct Electricity? A New Dataset for Open Book Question Answering. arXiv preprint arXiv:1809.02789.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: A multi-stage crowdsourcing pipeline on Amazon Mechanical Turk. Crowd-workers were shown a random science fact from a core set of 1,326 facts, asked to pair it with a second common fact to derive a new assertion, convert it into a question-answer pair, and add 3 incorrect choices. Questions passed basic checks (e.g., choice uniformity), were filtered using IR and word-association solvers to ensure hardness, evaluated by 5 crowd-workers for answerability (retaining those answered correctly by at least 4 out of 5), and their choices were randomly shuffled. Dev and Test sets were further filtered by an in-house expert.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: User-generated content data, Manual Human Curator
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: A subset of the WorldTree corpus (specifically filtered down from 2,287 facts marked as 'central' by Jansen et al., 2018 to 1,326 general facts).
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Rule-based filtering ensuring: 1) exactly 4 answer choices; 2) no negation words (e.g., no, none, not, isn't, doesn't, aren't, don't, won't, except, can't, shouldn't, wouldn't, couldn't, mustn't); 3) uniform answer choice length (all with at most 3 or at least 4 words). IR and word-association solver filtering ensured solvers could not easily answer them. Answer choices were randomly shuffled to eliminate position bias. Out of 8,140 generated questions, 2,183 were discarded due to failing the answerability verification step.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Crowd-workers generated questions and associated second facts, and provided answerability judgments (5 crowd-workers independently answered each question; at least 4 had to answer correctly for it to be retained). In-house expert annotation was used to filter the Dev and Test sets for higher quality.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Questions were deemed answerable and retained only if at least 4 out of 5 crowd-workers answered them correctly. Theoretical human accuracy was modeled and estimated using Hoeffding's Inequality to account for selection bias.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Amazon Mechanical Turk crowd-workers from North America with a 'masters' level qualification.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: Human bias in crowdsourced questions was analyzed: before shuffling, choice 'A' was the correct answer in 69% of questions; plausible answer detector baselines achieved 49.6% without seeing the question; an odd-one-out solver achieved 50.2% because incorrect answers created by workers tend to be homogeneous or share non-scientific terms uncharacteristic of the correct answer; in 21% of analyzed cases, crowdsourced questions did not actually require the core science fact to answer.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The second common-knowledge facts (K) provided by crowd-workers tend to be noisy (incomplete, over-complete, or only distantly related to the question), subjective, and should not be viewed as 'gold' facts; pre-trained models struggle when questions test concepts outside the core science domain; questions with options like 'all of these' or 'all but' pose reasoning difficulties.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Open book question answering, multi-hop reasoning, reading comprehension, science question answering. Split into 4,957 training, 500 development, and 500 test questions.
